idiom_name: interface extending JpaRepository / CrudRepository, implementation generated by Spring Data
implementation_notes: Spring Data JPA generates the implementation (SimpleJpaRepository) for an interface extending Repository<T, ID>, CrudRepository or JpaRepository: derived query methods are parsed from the method name, explicit queries are declared with @Query, and paging/sorting come from Pageable and Sort. The domain sees only the interface, and shared method sets go behind a @NoRepositoryBean base interface. The classic hand-written structure is unnecessary unless the query cannot be expressed - and then it belongs in one @Query method rather than in rebuilt plumbing.
pitfalls: Derived query methods are parsed at application start-up: a misspelled property fails the boot, not the call site, so keep the names covered by an integration test.

Each repository method runs in its own transaction by default (SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional); spreading one business operation over several calls commits partial state - put @Transactional on the application service.

Extending JpaRepository exposes flush, deleteAll and the EntityManager surface (getReference, flush); leaking those into the domain reintroduces the persistence coupling the repository was meant to remove.

variants.name: Hand-written repository over EntityManager (plain Jakarta Persistence)
variants.idiom_name: class implementing the domain interface with EntityManager + JPQL
variants.implementation_notes: Without Spring Data the repository is a hand-written final class holding an EntityManager (or a Provider<EntityManager>), implementing the domain interface with JPQL createQuery and persist/find/remove; the classic structure - interface, implementation, mapping delegated to the ORM - is fully visible. Choose it for plain Jakarta Persistence stacks or where per-call control (flush modes, lock modes, fetch graphs) cannot be expressed through generated proxies.
pitfalls: An EntityManager is not thread-safe and follows the persistence-context scope; a repository that caches it across requests corrupts the context and the identity map.
Calling em.flush() or committing inside the repository defeats the unit of work; leave flush and commit to the transaction boundary.
A JPQL query returning entities re-reads the persistence context automatically, but a native query does not: mixing the two makes read-modify-write behaviour inconsistent.
